concept.title: Symmetric Coloring Reduction Lemma for Hales-Jewett Line-Freeness
concept.concept_description: A coordinate-symmetric r-coloring of the cube [t]^n is line-free with respect to combinatorial lines having at most K active coordinates if and only if the induced coloring of the discrete simplex Δ(t-1, n) has no monochromatic corner tuple of width at most K. This equivalence reduces checking line-freeness of a symmetric coloring (a property of the exponentially large cube) to checking corner-tuple-freeness on the polynomially-sized simplex, and is the theoretical foundation enabling the certified lower bounds HJ(3,3) ≥ 22 and HJ(4,2) ≥ 14.
concept.mathematical_framing: A coordinate-symmetric r-coloring of the cube [t]^n is line-free with respect to combinatorial lines having at most K active coordinates if and only if the induced coloring of the discrete simplex Δ(t-1, n) has no monochromatic corner tuple of width at most K. This equivalence reduces checking line-freeness of a symmetric coloring (a property of the exponentially large cube) to checking corner-tuple-freeness on the polynomially-sized simplex, and is the theoretical foundation enabling the certified lower bounds HJ(3,3) ≥ 22 and HJ(4,2) ≥ 14.
concept.lean_guess: Formalize coordinate-symmetric colorings as functions on letter-count vectors (elements of the discrete simplex). Define corner tuples as the image of combinatorial lines under the letter-count map. The forward direction follows from the fact that a monochromatic line projects to a monochromatic corner tuple. The reverse direction uses the symmetry: if a corner tuple is monochromatic, the corresponding line (reconstructed by assigning active coordinates to the varying letter and fixed coordinates according to the count vector) is monochromatic in the original coloring by symmetry. The key invariant is that symmetric colorings factor through the letter-count projection.

1. **A complete sign characterization of the secret-key rate via the threshold.**
   Once a critical QBER `p*` (any zero of `secureKeyRate` on `[0, 1/2]`) is fixed,
   the secret-key rate is *positive exactly below* `p*` and *negative exactly above*
   it.  This converts the abstract IVT existence/uniqueness of `KeyRateThreshold`
   into the operational statement "secure ⟺ QBER < p*".

2. **The partial intercept–resend attack.**  If Eve intercepts only a fraction
   `μ ∈ [0,1]` of the qubits (forwarding the rest untouched), the induced QBER is
   exactly `μ/4`.  Hence the attack is *survivable for key distillation* iff
   `μ < 4 p*` — a quantitative interpolation between the benign channel (`μ = 0`,
   rate `= log 2`) and full interception (`μ = 1`, QBER `1/4`, insecure).

We also pin the two endpoints of the rate curve: `secureKeyRate 0 = log 2`
(one full secret bit per sifted round, in nats) and `secureKeyRate (1/2) = -log 2`
(a fully randomized channel leaks everything).

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer): The IVT threshold `p*` of `KeyRateThreshold` is not just
  *a* zero but a genuine *phase boundary*: `secureKeyRate Q > 0 ⟺ Q < p*` for all
  admissible `Q`. Moreover the textbook full-strength intercept–resend (QBER `1/4`)
  is the `μ = 1` endpoint of a one-parameter family with QBER `μ/4`, whose security
  boundary is the single inequality `μ < 4 p*`.

  monotonicity work: it says detectability is a clean dichotomy with no ambiguous
  middle regime. The `4 p*` factor places the survivable-interception cutoff at

namespace BB84

/-! ## Endpoints of the secret-key-rate curve -/

/-
On a noiseless, un-eavesdropped channel (`Q = 0`) the BB84 rate is `log 2`,
i.e. one full secret bit per sifted round (in nats).
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_zero : secureKeyRate 0 = Real.log 2 := by
  unfold secureKeyRate; rw [ Real.binEntropy_zero ] ; ring;

/-
The noiseless rate is strictly positive: secret key is distillable.
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_zero_pos : 0 < secureKeyRate 0 := by
  rw [ BB84.secureKeyRate_zero ] ; exact Real.log_pos ( by norm_num )

/-
On a fully randomized channel (`Q = 1/2`) the rate is `-log 2`.
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_half : secureKeyRate (1 / 2) = - Real.log 2 := by
  unfold secureKeyRate;
  unfold binEntropy; norm_num; ring;

/-
The fully-randomized rate is strictly negative: no key can be distilled.
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_half_neg : secureKeyRate (1 / 2) < 0 := by
  exact secureKeyRate_half.symm ▸ neg_neg_of_pos ( Real.log_pos ( by norm_num ) )

/-! ## Threshold as a phase boundary -/

/-
**Phase boundary (secure side).** Given any zero `p` of the secret-key rate on
`[0, 1/2]`, the rate is positive *exactly* below `p`: secure ⟺ QBER `< p*`.
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_pos_iff_lt_threshold {p Q : ℝ}
    (hp : p ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 2⁻¹) (hpz : secureKeyRate p = 0)
    (hQ : Q ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 2⁻¹) :
    0 < secureKeyRate Q ↔ Q < p := by
      constructor <;> intro h;
      · contrapose! h;
        cases eq_or_lt_of_le h <;> [ aesop; linarith [ secureKeyRate_strictAntiOn hp hQ ‹_› ] ];
      · linarith [ BB84.secureKeyRate_strictAntiOn hQ hp h ]

/-
**Phase boundary (insecure side).** With the same threshold `p`, the rate is
negative *exactly* above `p`: insecure ⟺ QBER `> p*`.
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_neg_iff_gt_threshold {p Q : ℝ}
    (hp : p ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 2⁻¹) (hpz : secureKeyRate p = 0)
    (hQ : Q ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 2⁻¹) :
    secureKeyRate Q < 0 ↔ p < Q := by
      constructor <;> intro h;
      · exact lt_of_not_ge fun h' => h.not_ge <| by linarith [ BB84.secureKeyRate_strictAntiOn.le_iff_ge ( by aesop ) ( by aesop ) |>.2 h' ] ;
      · exact hpz ▸ BB84.secureKeyRate_strictAntiOn hp hQ h

/-! ## Partial intercept–resend -/

/-- QBER induced when Eve intercepts (and resends) only a fraction `μ` of the qubits,
forwarding the remaining `1 - μ` untouched (error-free). The intercepted fraction
contributes the full intercept–resend error `interceptResendQBER a`. -/
def partialInterceptResendQBER (μ : ℝ) (a : Bool) : ℝ :=
  μ * interceptResendQBER a

/-
**Partial intercept–resend induces QBER `μ/4`.**
-/
theorem partialInterceptResendQBER_eq (μ : ℝ) (a : Bool) :
    partialInterceptResendQBER μ a = μ / 4 := by
      rw [ partialInterceptResendQBER, interceptResendQBER_eq, mul_one_div ]

/-
**Survivable-interception cutoff.** For an interception fraction `μ ∈ [0,1]` and
any threshold `p ∈ (1/16, 1/8)`, the secret-key rate stays positive *exactly* when
`μ < 4 p`: Eve may tap less than a `4 p* (≈ 44%)` fraction before the key becomes
undistillable.
-/
theorem partialInterceptResend_secure_iff (a : Bool) {μ p : ℝ}
    (hμ : μ ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) (hp : p ∈ Set.Ioo (1 / 16 : ℝ) (1 / 8))
    (hpz : secureKeyRate p = 0) :
    0 < secureKeyRate (partialInterceptResendQBER μ a) ↔ μ < 4 * p := by
      convert secureKeyRate_pos_iff_lt_threshold _ _ _ using 1;
      rotate_left;
      exact p;
      · constructor <;> norm_num at * <;> linarith;
      · exact hpz;
      · constructor <;> norm_num [ partialInterceptResendQBER_eq ] <;> nlinarith [ hμ.1, hμ.2, interceptResendQBER_eq a ];
      · rw [ partialInterceptResendQBER_eq ] ; constructor <;> intro <;> linarith

end BB84

# Discrete concavity and the interval property

This file develops the combinatorial heart of the *Interval Property for
Connected Slice-Projections of Polymatroids*.

A sequence `g : ℕ → ℤ` is **discretely concave** when its successive
differences are non-increasing.  The central result is that the *superlevel
set* `{ j | 0 < g j }` of a discretely concave sequence is an **interval**:
if `g a > 0` and `g c > 0` with `a ≤ b ≤ c`, then `g b > 0`.

This is exactly the abstract shape of the interval-property conjecture: the
slice-connectivity profile of a polymatroid element is discretely concave
(proved in `SliceInterval.lean`), so its connected slices form an interval.

We also prove that the property is a **strict** strengthening of the paper's
theorem "no two consecutive slice-projections are both disconnected", by
exhibiting a (non-concave) profile that satisfies the latter but not the
former.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): "Concavity of the marginal rank profile forces the
  connected-slice set to be an interval." Bold form: the interval property is
  *equivalent* to discrete concavity of the connectivity defect.
Experiment (Experimenter): Proved `min_le` (concave ⇒ dominates endpoint min)
  via the chord/telescoping inequality, then `superlevel_isInterval`.
Analysis (Analyst): The chord inequality `(c-a)·g b ≥ (c-b)·g a + (b-a)·g c`

Critique (Critic): Is the interval property trivial? No — the witness

  so concavity is doing genuine work.

namespace PolymatroidSlice

/-- A sequence `g : ℕ → ℤ` is *discretely concave* if its successive
differences `g (j+1) - g j` are non-increasing, equivalently
`g (j+2) + g j ≤ 2 * g (j+1)`. -/
def DiscreteConcave (g : ℕ → ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∀ j : ℕ, g (j + 2) + g j ≤ 2 * g (j + 1)

/-- Differences of a discretely concave sequence are antitone:
`g (j+1) - g j ≤ g (i+1) - g i` whenever `i ≤ j`. -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.diff_antitone {g : ℕ → ℤ} (hg : DiscreteConcave g)
    {i j : ℕ} (h : i ≤ j) :
    g (j + 1) - g j ≤ g (i + 1) - g i := by
  induction h <;> [ tauto; linarith [ hg ‹_› ] ]

/-- Chord inequality: a discretely concave sequence lies *above* its chords.
For `a ≤ b ≤ c`, `(c - a) · g b ≥ (c - b) · g a + (b - a) · g c`. -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.chord {g : ℕ → ℤ} (hg : DiscreteConcave g)
    {a b c : ℕ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c) :
    ((c : ℤ) - a) * g b ≥ ((c : ℤ) - b) * g a + ((b : ℤ) - a) * g c := by
  induction' hbc with k hk;
  · norm_num;
  · have h_diff : g b - g a ≥ (b - a) * (g (k + 1) - g k) := by
      have h_diff : ∀ i j : ℕ, i ≤ j → j ≤ k → g j - g i ≥ (j - i) * (g (k + 1) - g k) := by
        intros i j hij hjk; induction hij <;> simp_all +decide [ Nat.succ_eq_add_one ] ;
        have h_diff : g (k + 1) - g k ≤ g (Nat.succ ‹_›) - g ‹_› := by
          exact DiscreteConcave.diff_antitone hg ( by linarith );
        grind;
      exact h_diff a b hab hk;
    grind

/-- A discretely concave sequence dominates the minimum of its endpoints:
`min (g a) (g c) ≤ g b` for `a ≤ b ≤ c`. -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.min_le {g : ℕ → ℤ} (hg : DiscreteConcave g)
    {a b c : ℕ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c) :
    min (g a) (g c) ≤ g b := by
  by_cases hac : a = c;
  · grind;
  · have := DiscreteConcave.chord hg hab hbc;
    cases min_cases ( g a ) ( g c ) <;> nlinarith [ show ( a : ℤ ) < c by exact_mod_cast lt_of_le_of_ne ( by linarith ) hac ]

/-- **Interval property.** The superlevel set `{ j | 0 < g j }` of a discretely
concave sequence is an interval: if the endpoints are positive, so is every
point in between. -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.superlevel_isInterval {g : ℕ → ℤ}
    (hg : DiscreteConcave g) {a b c : ℕ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c)
    (ha : 0 < g a) (hc : 0 < g c) : 0 < g b := by
  have h := hg.min_le hab hbc
  have : 0 < min (g a) (g c) := lt_min ha hc
  exact lt_of_lt_of_le this h

/-- Discrete concavity is preserved by subtracting a constant (shifting the
threshold). -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.sub_const {g : ℕ → ℤ} (hg : DiscreteConcave g) (t : ℤ) :
    DiscreteConcave (fun j => g j - t) := by
  intro j
  have h := hg j
  dsimp only
  linarith

/-- The connected-slice set, as a `Set ℕ`. -/
def connectedSet (g : ℕ → ℤ) : Set ℕ := { j | 0 < g j }

/-- For a discretely concave `g`, `connectedSet g` is order-convex
(an interval): membership of the two endpoints implies membership of all
intermediate indices. -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.connectedSet_ordConnected {g : ℕ → ℤ}
    (hg : DiscreteConcave g) : (connectedSet g).OrdConnected := by
  constructor
  intro a ha c hc b hb
  exact hg.superlevel_isInterval hb.1 hb.2 ha hc

/-! ## The interval property is a strict strengthening

The paper's theorem says no two *consecutive* slices are both disconnected.
We show this does not imply the interval property, via a concrete profile. -/

/-- A profile `κ` "has no two consecutive disconnected slices" on `{0,…,n}`. -/
def NoTwoConsecutiveDisconnected (κ : ℕ → ℤ) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ j : ℕ, j + 1 ≤ n → 0 < κ j ∨ 0 < κ (j + 1)

/-- Witness profile on `{0,1,2}`: connected, disconnected, connected. -/
def breakProfile : ℕ → ℤ
  | 0 => 1
  | 1 => -1
  | 2 => 1
  | _ => 1

/-- The witness satisfies "no two consecutive disconnected". -/
theorem breakProfile_noTwoConsecutive :
    NoTwoConsecutiveDisconnected breakProfile 2 := by
  intro j hj
  have hj1 : j ≤ 1 := by omega
  interval_cases j
  · left; decide
  · right; decide

/-- Yet its connected set `{0,2}` is **not** an interval: index `1` is between
connected indices `0` and `2` but is disconnected. Hence the interval property
is strictly stronger than the paper's theorem, and (consistently) the witness
fails to be discretely concave. -/
theorem breakProfile_not_interval :
    0 < breakProfile 0 ∧ 0 < breakProfile 2 ∧ ¬ (0 < breakProfile 1) := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_⟩ <;> decide

/-- Consistency check: the witness is **not** discretely concave, matching the
mechanism that concavity is exactly what forces the interval property. -/
theorem breakProfile_not_concave : ¬ DiscreteConcave breakProfile := by
  intro h
  have := h 0
  revert this
  decide

We formalize integer polymatroids on a finite ground type and develop the
connectivity theory used by the slice-projection interval property.

  submodularity, giving uncrossing tools for connectivity arguments.

  i.e. submodularity against `∅`.  `diminishing_returns` is the marginal
  rephrasing that powers slice concavity downstream.

open Finset

namespace PolymatroidSlice

/-- An **integer polymatroid** on a finite type `α`: a normalized, monotone,
submodular rank function `f : Finset α → ℤ`. -/
structure Polymatroid (α : Type*) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] where
  /-- The rank function. -/
  f : Finset α → ℤ
  /-- Normalization. -/
  empty : f ∅ = 0
  /-- Monotonicity. -/
  mono : ∀ {A B : Finset α}, A ⊆ B → f A ≤ f B
  /-- Submodularity. -/
  submod : ∀ A B : Finset α, f (A ∪ B) + f (A ∩ B) ≤ f A + f B

namespace Polymatroid

variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (P : Polymatroid α)

/-- The rank function is non-negative. -/
theorem f_nonneg (A : Finset α) : 0 ≤ P.f A := by
  exact P.empty ▸ P.mono ( Finset.empty_subset _ )

/-- The connectivity function `λ A = f A + f Aᶜ - f univ`. -/
def lambda (A : Finset α) : ℤ := P.f A + P.f Aᶜ - P.f univ

/-- The connectivity function is non-negative (submodularity against `∅`). -/
theorem lambda_nonneg (A : Finset α) : 0 ≤ P.lambda A := by
  convert sub_nonneg_of_le _;
  · infer_instance;
  · convert P.submod A Aᶜ using 1 ; simp +decide [ P.empty ]

/-- The connectivity function is symmetric under complementation. -/
theorem lambda_compl (A : Finset α) : P.lambda Aᶜ = P.lambda A := by
  unfold Polymatroid.lambda; simp +decide [ add_comm, Finset.compl_eq_univ_sdiff ] ;

/-- **The connectivity function is submodular.** A genuine polymatroid theorem:
`λ (A ∪ B) + λ (A ∩ B) ≤ λ A + λ B`. -/
theorem lambda_submodular (A B : Finset α) :
    P.lambda (A ∪ B) + P.lambda (A ∩ B) ≤ P.lambda A + P.lambda B := by
  unfold Polymatroid.lambda; linarith [ P.submod A B, P.submod Aᶜ Bᶜ, show P.f ( Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ ) = P.f ( A ∩ B ) ᶜ by rw [ ← Finset.compl_inter ], show P.f ( Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ ) = P.f ( A ∪ B ) ᶜ by rw [ ← Finset.compl_union ] ] ;

/-- **Diminishing returns** (marginal submodularity): for `A ⊆ B` and
`x ∉ B`, the marginal gain of `x` over the larger set `B` is at most its
marginal gain over the smaller set `A`. -/
theorem diminishing_returns {A B : Finset α} (hAB : A ⊆ B) {x : α}
    (hx : x ∉ B) :
    P.f (insert x B) - P.f B ≤ P.f (insert x A) - P.f A := by
  have h_submod : P.f (insert x A ∪ B) + P.f (insert x A ∩ B) ≤ P.f (insert x A) + P.f B := by
    exact P.submod _ _;
  rw [ show insert x A ∪ B = insert x B from ?_, show insert x A ∩ B = A from ?_ ] at h_submod;
  · linarith;
  · grind;
  · grind

end Polymatroid

# Computational Evidence — Interval Property for Slice-Projections of Polymatroids

## 1. The conjecture, restated

For a connected polymatroid `P` and element `e` of rank `r = f({e})`, let
`κ(j)` (`0 ≤ j ≤ r`) be the connectivity defect of the `j`-th slice-projection
of `e`. Slice `j` is *connected* iff `κ(j) > 0`. The conjecture: the set
`{ j | κ(j) > 0 }` is a contiguous interval.

## 2. Structural mechanism we identified

The slice-projection rank profile of a single element expanded into `r`
parallel copies is the function `g(j) = f(S_j)`, where `S_j` is the base set
together with `j` of the copies. By **submodularity (diminishing returns)**,
the marginal gains `g(j+1) - g(j)` are **non-increasing**, i.e. `g` is
*discretely concave*:

```
g(j+2) + g(j) ≤ 2 · g(j+1).
```

The slice connectivity `κ(j)` is a *minimum of affine-in-`j` functions* built
from these profiles, hence itself discretely concave. The key combinatorial
fact is:

> For a discretely concave integer sequence `g`, the superlevel set
> `{ j | g(j) > 0 }` is an interval.

This is because concavity gives `min(g a, g c) ≤ g b` whenever `a ≤ b ≤ c`.

## 3. Small-case calculations (concavity of marginal profiles)

Take `f` = rank of a polymatroid on copies of one element, `g(j) = min(j, 3)`
(a single element of rank 3, i.e. `f` saturates at 3):

| j      | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|--------|---|---|---|---|---|
| g(j)   | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| Δg     |   | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

Differences `1,1,1,0` are non-increasing ⇒ discretely concave. ✓

Connectivity defect samples `κ(j) = min(g(j), g(r)-g(j))` style envelopes are
unimodal, and their positive sets are always intervals in every sample tested.

## 4. Counterexample hunt — the conjecture is a *strict* strengthening

The paper's theorem ("no two consecutive slice-projections are both
disconnected") is **strictly weaker** than the interval property. Witness on
indices `{0,1,2}`:

```
κ = [ 1, -1, 1 ]      (connected, disconnected, connected)
```

* No two consecutive disconnected: only index `1` is disconnected. ✓ (paper's thm)
* Interval property: connected set `{0, 2}` is **not** an interval. ✗

Hence the paper's theorem alone cannot yield the interval property — genuine
polymatroid structure (the discrete concavity above) is required. This
`κ = [1,-1,1]` sequence is *not* discretely concave (`κ(2)+κ(0)=2 > 2·κ(1)=-2`),
consistent with the mechanism in §2.

## 5. Conclusion

All sampled discretely-concave profiles satisfy the interval property; the
only way to break it (the `[1,-1,1]` witness) also breaks concavity. This
pins the conjecture's truth to the *concavity of polymatroid rank profiles*,
which we formalize and prove in Lean.

*connectivity defect* of the `j`-th slice-projection,

would prove the conjecture in full generality, beyond the rank-profile model.

**The key insight is** that `κ` is a *minimum of functions that are affine in
the slice index `j`* (each partition contributes `f(A) + f(B) − f(E)` plus a
term linear in `j` from how `e`'s `r` units are split), and a minimum of affine
(hence concave) functions is concave — exactly the hypothesis our interval
criterion consumes.

**Why now?** We have already formalized both halves of the bridge: "concavity ⇒
interval" (`superlevel_isInterval`) and "polymatroid marginals are concave"
(`slice_profile_concave` via `diminishing_returns`). Only the min-over-partitions
assembly remains, and `lambda_submodular` provides the uncrossing needed to
control those partitions.

**Statement.** Among all integer profiles `κ : {0,…,r} → ℤ` arising as slice
connectivity defects of connected polymatroids, the interval property holds for

**The key insight is** that `breakProfile = [1,−1,1]` is simultaneously the
minimal interval-property violator and a minimal concavity violator
(`breakProfile_not_concave`), suggesting concavity is not just sufficient but

produced an explicit witness for the failure direction; closing the equivalence

upgrades to a precise two-block structure.

**Why now?** With the interval property established for the rank-profile model,
the prefix/suffix decomposition is a direct corollary; quantifying the block

concave; combining the two is the natural quantitative refinement of the
qualitative interval property.
